hints: Think about where the incoming nitro group can attack on methylbenzene relative to the methyl group to give the para product shown and what other position is similarly activated.
walkthrough:
Recall how methyl directs attack**
The $\text{CH}_3$ group is 2,4 directing, so it activates the ortho (2 and 6) and para (4) positions toward electrophiles. The diagram shows the para product, 4-nitromethylbenzene, so look for the other activated position.
Final answer: Benzene ring with $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{NO}_2$ in 1,2 (ortho) positions, 2-nitromethylbenzene.

hints: Remember that concentrated sulfuric acid acts as an acid toward nitric acid to generate the strong electrophile for nitration.
walkthrough:
Build the electrophile equation**
Nitration needs $\text{NO}_2^+$. Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which then loses water. Balancing with two $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives the nitronium ion plus oxonium and hydrogensulfate ions: $\text{HNO}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + 2\text{HSO}_4^-$.

hints: Compare the continuous pi system of methylbenzene with what happens when one ring carbon bonds to both H and NO2 in intermediate T.
Count how many pi electrons remain delocalised in T versus the six in methylbenzene.
Think about the hybridisation and geometry of the carbon that is attacked compared with a normal aromatic carbon.
walkthrough:
See the loss of the full ring**
In methylbenzene the six p orbitals overlap continuously around the ring, giving six delocalised pi electrons. In T the electrophile has added to one carbon, so that carbon now has four sigma bonds (to $\text{CH}$ ring bonds, to H and to $\text{NO}_2$). It cannot contribute a p orbital, so delocalisation is interrupted and extends over only five carbons.

Count electrons and hybridisation**
That means only four pi electrons remain in the delocalised system of T, two fewer than in methylbenzene. The attacked carbon has changed from trigonal planar $\text{sp}^2$ to tetrahedral $\text{sp}^3$, with bond angle about $109.5^\circ$ instead of $120^\circ$.

Link to bond equality**
Because aromaticity is lost, the C-C bonds in T are no longer all the same length and strength, unlike the equal bonds in methylbenzene. Any three of these contrast points earns full credit.

Final answer: Any three from:
Delocalisation extends over only five carbons in T, not six, pi system is partially broken.
T has only four pi electrons delocalised, methylbenzene has six.
One carbon is $\text{sp}^3$ hybridised in T, all carbons are $\text{sp}^2$ in methylbenzene.
One carbon is tetrahedral with bond angle $109.5^\circ$ in T, or C-C bonds are no longer all equal in length and angles are not all $120^\circ$.

hints: Identify the two functional groups on the para disubstituted benzene in W and number to give the acid carbon as position 1.
walkthrough:
Name the para acid amine**
W has $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{NH}_2$ para to each other. The carboxylic acid has priority, so the parent is benzoic acid with an amino substituent at position 4: 4-aminobenzoic acid.

hints: Start with step 1 converting nitro to amine and recall the classic metal plus acid reducing mixture for this change.
Think why the amine is protected as an amide in step 2 before strong oxidation, and which acyl chloride is used.
Consider what strong hot oxidant converts a methyl side chain to a carboxylic acid in step 3 without attacking the protected amide.
Recall how an amide protecting group is removed by acid hydrolysis in step 4.
Think about how a carboxylic acid is converted to an ethyl ester in step 5.
Add the specific conditions of heat, reflux or concentrated reagents that accompany each of these transformations.
walkthrough:
Reduce then protect**
Step 1 is $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$. Use $\text{Sn}$ with concentrated $\text{HCl}$ under reflux with heat. You must then protect the $\text{NH}_2$ because hot $\text{KMnO}_4$ would oxidise a free amine. Step 2 therefore uses ethanoyl chloride, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$, to give the amide $\text{NHCOCH}_3$.

Oxidise the side chain**
Step 3 oxidises the $\text{CH}_3$ attached to the ring to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ while the amide survives. Use hot acidified or alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ with heat. This is the classic alkylbenzene to benzoic acid oxidation.

Deprotect then esterify**
Step 4 regenerates the amine by acid hydrolysis of the amide: aqueous $\text{HCl}$ with heat to give W. Step 5 is Fischer esterification of the acid to the ethyl ester benzocaine: ethanol with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst, reflux and heat.

hints: Compare the environment of the nitrogen lone pair in aromatic benzocaine with that in aliphatic ethylamine.
Think about delocalisation into the benzene ring versus the electron donating effect of an alkyl group on proton acceptance.
walkthrough:
Judge lone pair availability**
Basicity means ability to accept $\text{H}^+$ using the nitrogen lone pair. In benzocaine the $\text{NH}_2$ is directly attached to the benzene ring, so its lone pair overlaps with the pi system and is delocalised over the ring. It is much less available.

Contrast with ethylamine**
In ethylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, there is no delocalisation and the ethyl alkyl group pushes electron density toward N by the inductive effect. The lone pair is more available, so ethylamine is the stronger base.

Final answer: Benzocaine is less basic than ethylamine as its N lone pair is less available to accept $\text{H}^+$.
In benzocaine the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring / phenyl is electron withdrawing, whereas in ethylamine the ethyl group is electron donating, increasing lone pair availability.

hints: Look for symmetry in the para disubstituted ring and count unique ring carbons plus the two ester carbons.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbons**
Benzocaine is para disubstituted, so the ring has a plane of symmetry giving 4 distinct ring carbon environments. Add the carbonyl C, the $\text{OCH}_2$ C and the $\text{CH}_3$ C, all different. Total $4 + 3 = 7$ peaks in the $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectrum.
Final answer: 7 peaks

hints: Think about what nucleus proton NMR detects and whether CDCl3 contains that isotope.
walkthrough:
Why deuterate the solvent**
Proton NMR detects $^1\text{H}$ only, not D ($^2\text{H}$). $\text{CDCl}_3$ has no $^1\text{H}$ so it is silent, while $\text{CHCl}_3$ contains $^1\text{H}$ and would produce its own peak that could hide sample peaks.
Final answer: $\text{CDCl}_3$ gives no signal in $^1\text{H}$ NMR whereas $\text{CHCl}_3$ would give a signal and interfere.

hints: Use the Data Booklet ranges to match the high field alkyl signals near 1.2 and 3.5 ppm to the ethyl ester group.
Recall where N-H protons typically appear and what splitting they show due to lack of coupling.
Think about the aromatic protons near 7 ppm and why para disubstitution gives four protons in a complex pattern.
Apply the n+1 rule to the CH3-CH2 pair to assign triplet versus quartet and count hydrogens.
walkthrough:
Assign the ethyl ester pair**
The $\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ group gives two signals. The $\text{CH}_3$ next to $\text{CH}_2$ appears at $\delta$ 1.2, integrates to 3 H and is split to a triplet. The $\text{OCH}_2$ is more deshielded by O at $\delta$ 3.5, integrates to 2 H and is split to a quartet.

Assign NH2 and aromatic H**
The $\text{NH}_2$ protons appear at $\delta$ 5.5, 2 H, as a broad singlet with no coupling to neighbours. The four ring protons appear downfield at $\delta$ 7.1 to 7.4, 4 H, as a multiplet due to complex aromatic coupling.

hints: Focus on the protons on the carbon next to the CH3 group responsible for the 1.2 ppm signal.
walkthrough:
Apply n+1**
The $\delta$ 1.2 $\text{CH}_3$ is next to the $\text{OCH}_2$ group which has two equivalent protons. Using n+1, $2+1 = 3$, so the signal is split into a triplet.
Final answer: Triplet because adjacent / neighbouring carbon has two H atoms ($\text{CH}_2$), n+1 = 3.

hints: Remember which protons are labile and exchange with D2O and what that means for their NMR signal.
walkthrough:
Spot the exchangeable protons**
$\text{N-H}$ protons are labile and swap with D from $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ to give N-D. Deuterium is invisible in proton NMR, so the $\delta$ 5.5 $\text{NH}_2$ signal disappears.
Final answer: Peak at $\delta$ 5.5 / $\text{NH}_2$ peak disappears as $\text{NH}_2$ protons exchange with deuterium.

hints: Recall the low temperature reagents that convert a primary aromatic amine to a diazonium salt.
walkthrough:
Choose diazotisation reagents**
Primary aromatic amines form diazonium salts with nitrous acid generated in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid, $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$, kept cold below $10^\circ\text{C}$.
Final answer: $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$ (or $\text{HNO}_2$), below $10^\circ\text{C}$.

hints: Think about what functional group replaces the NH2 of benzocaine after diazotisation in R.
Consider how the diazonium ion couples with phenol in alkaline solution to form the N=N link in S and at which ring position.
walkthrough:
Draw R then couple to S**
R is the diazonium salt from benzocaine: keep the para $\text{CO}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ group and replace $\text{NH}_2$ by $\text{N}^+ \equiv \text{N}$, so $\text{CO}_2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}^+ \equiv \text{N}$.

Form the azo dye**
In step 2 this couples with phenol in $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ at the para position to the $\text{OH}$ (phenoxide is strongly activating). Join the two rings with $\text{N=N}$ to give $\text{CO}_2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$.

Final answer: R: $p\text{-CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}^+ \equiv \text{N}$ (para ester benzene diazonium ion);
S: $p\text{-CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$ para to OH (azo dye).
